conclusion.justification: The report concludes with a 'no—not as a general conclusion', citing high-quality Cochrane evidence showing no evidence of reduced duration and guidelines recommending against routine use, while acknowledging some low-certainty nuances for specific strains.
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
**Conclusion: no—not as a general conclusion.** Earlier, smaller trials and meta-analyses often found that probiotics shortened acute infectious diarrhea (typically by less than a day), but the apparent benefit varied substantially by study and probiotic strain. More rigorous evidence changes the interpretation: the 2020 Cochrane review found that probiotics *may not* affect duration, and that it is uncertain whether they shorten time to recovery. In analyses restricted to the large, low-risk-of-bias trials, there was no evidence of reduced duration.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD003048/INFECTN_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/

**Why the answer is not straightforward:** “Probiotics” are not one treatment. Effects, if any, depend on the exact organism/strain, dose, setting, diarrhea cause, and patient population. Thus positive results from a particular strain or older study should not be assumed to apply to an over-the-counter product generally, or to adults and children alike.

**Guidelines reflect this uncertainty.** The American Gastroenterological Association suggests *against* probiotics for children with acute infectious gastroenteritis (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), consistent with the newer high-quality trials.  
https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext

By contrast, ESPGHAN says clinicians *may* recommend specific strains—e.g., *Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus* GG, at ≥10¹⁰ CFU/day for 5–7 days—for childhood acute gastroenteritis, but labels the evidence for reduced diarrhea duration **low certainty**.  
https://www.espghan.org/dam/jcr:299e3330-b1b6-4940-aa72-786501bffff1/2023_Probiotics+for+the+Management+of+Pediatric+Gastrointestinal+Disorders:+Position+Paper+of+the+ESPGHAN+Special+Interest+Group+on+Gut+Microbiota+and+Modifications.pdf

So, probiotics should not be expected to reliably shorten acute infectious diarrhea; rehydration remains the central treatment.
